reports.report: I analyzed the problem by modeling it as a minimum edge coverage problem on a grid. Each 2x2 block must contain at least one pair of cells with the same color. I showed that each such pair (represented as an edge in the grid graph) can satisfy at most 2 blocks. For an $n \times n$ grid, there are $(n-1)^2$ blocks, requiring at least $\lceil (n-1)^2 / 2 \rceil$ edges. For $n=100$, this is $\lceil 99^2 / 2 \rceil = 4901$ edges. The number of colors is then $n^2 - 4901 = 10000 - 4901 = 5099$. I verified this for small $n$ (e.g., $n=2$ gives 3, $n=3$ gives 7, $n=4$ gives 11).

This is equivalent to finding a set of equalities (same-colored adjacent pairs) that covers all 9801 2x2 blocks in a 100x100 grid. 9. The formula $n^2 - \lceil (n-1)^2/2 \rceil$ seems robust.

args.report: I analyzed the problem by modeling it as a minimum edge coverage problem on a grid. Each 2x2 block must contain at least one pair of cells with the same color. I showed that each such pair (represented as an edge in the grid graph) can satisfy at most 2 blocks. For an $n \times n$ grid, there are $(n-1)^2$ blocks, requiring at least $\lceil (n-1)^2 / 2 \rceil$ edges. For $n=100$, this is $\lceil 99^2 / 2 \rceil = 4901$ edges. The number of colors is then $n^2 - 4901 = 10000 - 4901 = 5099$. I verified this for small $n$ (e.g., $n=2$ gives 3, $n=3$ gives 7, $n=4$ gives 11).
